title: What is fault tolerance, and how is it achieved using the replication factor (leader election, ISR, acks)?
shortTitle: Fault tolerance in Kafka through the replication factor

s1_definition.profdef: Fault tolerance is a system's ability to keep operating correctly and without data loss despite the failure of some of its components. Kafka achieves fault tolerance primarily through replication: each partition is copied across several brokers using the replication factor, so the failure of one or more brokers does not lose data or stop the topic. The three mechanisms that work together are the replication factor (how many copies exist), the in-sync replica set with leader election (a caught-up replica is promoted when the leader fails), and producer acknowledgments (acks=all with min.insync.replicas ensures a write is on enough copies before it is confirmed).
s1_definition.analogy: Fault tolerance is like National Bank of India staying open even when things break. The bank keeps three copies of each ledger drawer in three different vaults (replication factor). It only tells a customer "your deposit is confirmed" after at least two vaults have recorded it (acks and min.insync.replicas). If the main vault burns down, the bank immediately promotes one of the up-to-date copies to be the new main vault (leader election from the ISR). The customer never notices, and no record is lost. That seamless survival is fault tolerance.
s1_definition.oneliner: Fault tolerance is surviving failures without loss, and Kafka gets it from replication, ISR-based leader election, and acks=all with min.insync.replicas.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Fault tolerance is a system's ability to keep operating correctly and without data loss despite the failure of some of its components. Kafka achieves fault tolerance primarily through replication: each partition is copied across several brokers using the replication factor, so the failure of one or more brokers does not lose data or stop the topic. The three mechanisms that work together are the replication factor (how many copies exist), the in-sync replica set with leader election (a caught-up replica is promoted when the leader fails), and producer acknowledgments (acks=all with min.insync.replicas ensures a write is on enough copies before it is confirmed).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Fault tolerance is like National Bank of India staying open even when things break. The bank keeps three copies of each ledger drawer in three different vaults (replication factor). It only tells a customer "your deposit is confirmed" after at least two vaults have recorded it (acks and min.insync.replicas). If the main vault burns down, the bank immediately promotes one of the up-to-date copies to be the new main vault (leader election from the ISR). The customer never notices, and no record is lost. That seamless survival is fault tolerance.

**One line to remember:** Fault tolerance is surviving failures without loss, and Kafka gets it from replication, ISR-based leader election, and acks=all with min.insync.replicas.

sections.s2_technical:
Fault tolerance in distributed systems means two things: durability, so committed data is never lost, and availability, so the service keeps responding even when components fail. Kafka delivers both for partitioned topics through replication, and the replication factor is the foundation. With a replication factor of three, every partition exists as three copies on three brokers, so losing one or even two brokers still leaves a copy.

The first mechanism is the replication factor itself. It sets the redundancy. A replication factor of N tolerates up to N minus one simultaneous broker failures without losing the partition's data. If you had a replication factor of one, a single broker failure would lose and stop that partition, so one provides no fault tolerance. Three is the production norm because it balances safety and cost.

The second mechanism is the in-sync replica set and leader election. The ISR is the leader plus all followers caught up within the lag window. When the leader's broker fails, the controller promotes a new leader from the ISR, never from a lagging replica (unless unclean election is explicitly enabled, which risks data loss). Because every ISR member has all committed records, the new leader has the full committed history, so failover preserves data and resumes service quickly. This is the availability half of fault tolerance — the partition keeps serving through a leader change.

The third mechanism is producer acknowledgments combined with min.insync.replicas. The acks setting controls when a producer considers a write successful. With acks=0 the producer does not wait at all and can lose data; with acks=1 the leader acknowledges after writing locally, so a leader crash before followers copy the record loses it; with acks=all the leader acknowledges only after every replica in the ISR has copied the record. Pairing acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 means a write is confirmed only when it exists on at least two brokers, and if the ISR shrinks below two the leader rejects writes rather than risk loss. This is the durability half of fault tolerance — a confirmed write survives a broker failure.

These three mechanisms must be configured together to actually get fault tolerance. Replication factor three alone is not enough if the producer uses acks=1, because a record acknowledged by only the leader can vanish if the leader dies before followers copy it. Likewise acks=all is not enough with a replication factor of one, because there is only one copy. The correct fault-tolerant recipe for banking is replication factor three, min.insync.replicas two, acks=all, and unclean leader election disabled.

The senior-level nuance is understanding the failure scenarios and the trade-offs. With this recipe you survive one broker failure fully — writes continue and no data is lost. If two of the three brokers fail, the ISR drops below min.insync.replicas, so the leader stops accepting writes to protect durability, meaning you sacrifice availability to avoid loss. You also plan replica placement across racks or availability zones so a whole-zone outage still leaves a copy, and you monitor under-replicated partitions and ISR shrink events because they are early warnings that your fault tolerance margin is eroding.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India must prove that a confirmed transfer survives broker failures, and the team builds a simulation that exercises the three fault-tolerance mechanisms together.

Problem 1 — When a transfer is confirmed to the customer, it must never be lost even if a broker crashes right after. This is exactly acks=all with min.insync.replicas two — the write is confirmed only after it lives on at least two brokers.

Problem 2 — When the leader broker for a partition crashes, transfers must keep being processed within seconds. This is exactly leader election from the ISR — a caught-up replica takes over.

Problem 3 — If too many brokers fail at once, the bank must stop confirming new transfers rather than risk losing them. This is exactly the min.insync.replicas guard — the leader rejects writes when the ISR is too small.

The mini-project is a fault-tolerance simulator. We build a `TransferEvent` domain object, a `BrokerReplica` with a log and health flag, a `FaultTolerantPartition` that tracks the ISR and performs leader election, and a `DurabilityManager` that confirms writes only under acks=all and min.insync.replicas. The demo confirms a transfer, kills the leader to show failover, then kills a second broker to show writes being rejected to protect durability.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is three transfers TXF-1, TXF-2, TXF-3, with a partition of replication factor three and min.insync.replicas two.

Step 1 — The partition starts with leader broker-1 and followers broker-2 and broker-3, all alive, so the ISR is three brokers.

Step 2 — TXF-1 is confirmed with acks=all. The manager checks the ISR size is three, which meets the minimum of two, so it replicates TXF-1 to all three brokers and confirms it. The log notes the transfer now survives two more failures.

Step 3 — broker-1, the leader, crashes. The partition elects a new leader from the ISR; broker-2 is alive and caught up, so it becomes the leader with no committed data lost. The ISR is now broker-2 and broker-3.

Step 4 — TXF-2 is confirmed. The ISR size is two, which still meets the minimum of two, so TXF-2 replicates to both surviving brokers and is confirmed. Service continued through the leader failure, demonstrating availability without loss.

Step 5 — broker-2 crashes too. Now only broker-3 is alive, so the ISR size is one, below the minimum of two. TXF-3 is rejected. The bank deliberately stops confirming new transfers because it cannot guarantee durability with only one copy. This shows the final trade-off: when the fault-tolerance margin is exhausted, Kafka sacrifices availability to protect durability.

```
  Producer: confirmTransfer(acks=all)
    │ confirm ONLY if ISR >= min.insync.replicas(2)
    ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Partition (RF=3)                                          │
  │  broker-1[LEADER] ─ broker-2[ISR] ─ broker-3[ISR]         │
  │  TXF-1 → copied to all 3 → CONFIRMED                      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    │ broker-1 crashes
    ▼
  elect leader from ISR → broker-2[LEADER] ─ broker-3[ISR]  (ISR=2)
  TXF-2 → copied to 2 → CONFIRMED (survives 1 more failure)
    │ broker-2 crashes
    ▼
  ISR = { broker-3 } size 1 < minInSync 2
  TXF-3 → REJECTED  (availability sacrificed to protect durability)
```

       → another dies → [ISR=1 < minInSync] → [WRITES REJECTED]
       → broker recovers + catches up → [ISR grows] → writable again

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────────

  1. mgr.confirmTransfer(TXF-1) → ISR=3 ≥ 2 → replicate → CONFIRM
  2. partition.killBroker("broker-1"); electLeaderFromIsr() → broker-2
  3. mgr.confirmTransfer(TXF-2) → ISR=2 ≥ 2 → CONFIRM
  4. partition.killBroker("broker-2")
  5. mgr.confirmTransfer(TXF-3) → ISR=1 < 2 → REJECT

  Contract for confirmTransfer(event):
    Pre:  none
    Post: confirmed only if ISR ≥ minInSync and all ISR copied it
    Rule: reject rather than risk losing a confirmed transfer

sections.s6_takeaway:
Fault tolerance is a system's ability to keep running correctly and without losing data even when some of its components fail. In Kafka, fault tolerance for topics is achieved through replication, and three mechanisms work together to deliver it: the replication factor, the in-sync replica set with leader election, and producer acknowledgments with min.insync.replicas.

The replication factor provides the redundancy. With a replication factor of three, each partition has three copies on three brokers, so the topic survives up to two broker failures. The in-sync replica set and leader election provide availability: the ISR is the leader plus the caught-up followers, and when the leader's broker dies the controller promotes a new leader from the ISR, which has every committed record, so service resumes with no data loss. Producer acknowledgments provide durability: with acks=all the leader confirms a write only after every ISR member has copied it, and min.insync.replicas sets the floor, so if the ISR shrinks below that floor the leader refuses writes instead of risking loss.

The crucial point I always stress is that these must be configured together. Replication factor three with acks=1 is not truly fault tolerant, because a record acknowledged only by the leader can vanish if the leader dies before followers copy it. The correct banking recipe is replication factor three, min.insync.replicas two, acks=all, and unclean leader election disabled. With that setup you fully survive one broker failure — writes continue and nothing is lost — and if two of three brokers fail, Kafka deliberately stops confirming new writes to protect durability, trading availability for safety.

In my banking platform at National Bank of India, every money-movement topic uses exactly this configuration, so a confirmed transfer always lives on at least two brokers and survives a broker crash, and a leader failure triggers a seamless election that keeps processing transfers within seconds. The senior insight is that fault tolerance is not a single switch but a balance of durability, availability, and latency, and for money I always lean toward durability while monitoring under-replicated partitions and ISR-shrink alerts as early warnings that my safety margin is eroding.

---

keyPoints: Replication factor: copies of each partition across brokers
ISR (In-Sync Replicas): followers caught up with leader
acks=all: wait for all ISR to acknowledge — strongest durability
